catalog_quote: Stress assignment is best explained on the basis of metrical patterns (cf. Hayes 1995). It is similar to the stress patterns found in the Mojeño languages (de Carvalho & Rose 2018, Rose 2019c) and usually follows an iambic pattern with left-to-right parsing, which is sensitive to morae (§3.6.1). The last syllable of a word is always extrametrical, i.e. it is “invisible” for stress parsing. Morae are organised into feet, and primary stress is usually found on the last foot of the word, sometimes on the last foot that belongs to the word stem, depending on how many markers are attached. Secondary stress is on every other foot. Bimoraic words have a trochaic pattern for stress assignment (§3.6.2). When grammatical markers are attached to the word stem, the metrical pattern of the stem is maintained ... [p.108] That parsing is sensitive to morae and not to syllables becomes apparent when co…

audit.reasoning: The record rests on the only full reference grammar of the language (Terhart 2024, 813 pp., open access), which we hold, and the deciding quotation is verbatim at the cited pages (pp. 106 and 108 within §3.6, pp. 105-111). The classification 'weight-hedged' (mora-counting left-to-right iambs, final-syllable extrametricality, primary stress on the last foot, diphthong syllables bimoraic, bimoraic words trochaic, author's 'usually' plus listed exception classes in (82)-(84) and Table 3.19) matches the source's own hedged metrical statement. The two other Glottolog items are the same author's earlier dissertation and a 2014 Spanish sketch, both superseded; no independent phonology/instrumental study exists to my knowledge from the pages and bibliographic records opened.
